summary:
Manipur stands under India's national framework: no region-specific trans statute, recognition scheme or enforcement campaign specific to Manipur is reported in the sources. The operative law is the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 as amended in 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the self-identification route that the 2019 law had provided and that the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling established, and restricts legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex persons. Recognition now turns on biological or physical traits, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery before an identity is granted. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

The narrowed scheme excludes trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the accepted categories. The government presents the narrower definition as concentrating welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection on recognised groups; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as an attack on the right to exist, and critics warn that many trans and gender-fluid people are left outside any recognition. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The amendment also creates offences including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to become transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that this provision could be used against support networks and organisations that assist trans people.

Recognition is thin on the ground: of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 amendment sits within a wider direction of travel in Indian law rather than an isolated measure: the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita already removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences, and trans communities report expecting more assaults under the new code. A visitor assessing risk should read the two changes together.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented nationally across rail, air and passport channels, with incidents in Kolkata, Assam and Chennai in 2024 and a passport-related court ruling in February 2026. The pattern is one of administrative encounters, not only statutory text, and the same class of encounter applies at Manipur's airports and railway stations.

Protection is unevenly distributed. The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police and the Allahabad High Court's February 2026 relief on passport medical examinations show active high-court intervention, while the UK Home Office's December 2025 note rates police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, more likely in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Comparatively, the 2014 Supreme Court recognition of self-identification placed India among jurisdictions granting legal gender recognition on a self-declared basis; the March 2026 amendment moves the country toward the medical-certification model common in narrower recognition regimes.
localsOnly:
Identity documentation for residents runs through the certificate-and-card system under the 2019 Act as amended: medical boards and district authorities now certify gender-affirming surgery, and only historically recognised groups such as hijra and kinner, plus intersex persons, qualify for recognition. Trans men, trans women and non-binary residents who self-identify outside those categories have no route to a recognised identity document.

Only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons hold identity cards, so most residents, including in Manipur, live without the documentation that gates access to welfare schemes, shelters and reservation-linked benefits.

The government's stated purpose for the narrower definition is to concentrate welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection. The new offence of coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, carrying up to life imprisonment, applies to conduct within the community as well as outside it, and Human Rights Watch warns it may reach support networks and community organisations.

Residents face the same criminal-law landscape as elsewhere in India: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in force since 2024 lacks the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence provisions of the repealed Indian Penal Code. Police sensitisation obligations derive from the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines, which are binding in that court's jurisdiction and influential nationally.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was still pending as of late March 2026; the sources do not record whether assent has since been given, and the operative status of the amendment at the time of reading is therefore unresolved.

No source in the inventory reports Manipur-specific enforcement, state implementation rules, Manipur police conduct toward trans people, or the number of identity cards issued in Manipur. The absence of Manipur-level reporting is an absence of sourcing, not evidence of no incidents.

Incident data on checkpoint friction comes from Kolkata, Assam and Chennai; whether comparable encounters occur at Imphal airport or on Manipur's rail network is not sourced here.

The scale of the exclusion created by the March 2026 amendment, including how many people in Manipur fall outside the recognised categories, is not quantified in the sources.
